vignette:
He remembers the sound first. Not the words, not the thud of fist against bone, but the wet, ragged breathing that followed—his mother gasping in the kitchen, his father standing over her, knuckles white. He was six, maybe seven, crouched behind the living room sofa, watching through the gap between the cushions. He held his breath the way he always did, waiting for it to end. It always ended. But the sound never left.

Now he is eighteen, the youngest project manager in his company’s history. People call him mature, composed. He manages a small team of five, coordinates timelines, flags risks before they escalate. On the surface, it looks like competence. Underneath, it is a constant, exhausting calculation: if I control every variable, nothing bad will happen. When a teammate misses a deadline, his chest tightens. When a stakeholder raises their voice in a meeting, his vision narrows. He does not shout. He freezes—then politely excuses himself to the bathroom, where he splashes water on his face and tells his reflection, *You are not a child anymore.*

He is in a relationship with a girl named Leilani. She is patient, kind, the first person he has told about the shouting. But he does not tell her everything. When she playfully raises her voice while teasing him, he flinches—just a flicker, barely noticeable—and she notices anyway. She asks what is wrong, and he says, “Nothing, just tired.” He is always tired. Sleep comes hard; his bedroom door must be unlocked, because locked doors remind him of nights he pressed his ear to his own door, trying to hear if it was safe to come out. He wakes often, heart pounding, convinced someone is fighting in the next room, even though he lives alone.

At work, his hypervigilance looks like diligence. He double-checks every email, re-reads meeting notes three times. But his concentration bleeds; two hours into a planning session, he loses the thread of conversation because a sudden overhead announcement (like a door slamming) yanks him back. He dissociates during routine task updates, his mind drifting to a kitchen floor he has not seen in over a decade. Once, his boss called his name three times before he responded.

He avoids arguments. Not just loud ones—any conflict. If a disagreement arises on his team, he mediates with careful words, smoothing tension before it can rise in pitch. He cannot tolerate raised voices. His stomach churns. His hands shake. He would rather absorb blame than let a confrontation escalate.

Leilani wants him to meet her family. He is terrified. Not of them—of the possibility that her father might argue with her mother, that the voices might rise, that he might have to leave the room. He has already started planning an escape route: the bathroom near the back door, the park bench outside, his car keys in his pocket.

He does not think of himself as traumatized. He thinks of himself as careful. He thinks of himself as someone who keeps things under control. But the PCL-5 score of 55, if he ever saw it, would tell a different story—intrusive images of his mother’s face, avoidant behaviors he cannot name, a relentless sense of threat even in safe places. He carries the sound of that ragged breathing in the rhythm of his own. Sometimes, late at night, he sits on the edge of his bed and listens to the silence of his apartment, testing it like a bruise. It is quiet. It is always quiet. And he still cannot believe it will stay that way.
